screens.title: Centralized Data Policies in SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on centralized data policies and why they are the heart of SD‑WAN forwarding decisions. Centralized data policies are configured in vManage, distributed by vSmart, and enforced at the edge by vEdge or cEdge devices. These policies act on the data plane: they classify traffic, assign SLA expectations, mark packets for QoS, and implement security rules like zone‑based firewalls. You will learn how Application‑Aware Routing uses SLA classes to pick the best transport, how QoS uses classification and DSCP marking to prioritize flows, and how firewall zone pairs protect branches. A concrete example you'll see repeatedly is prioritizing Voice traffic: voice is identified, set to an SLA class, DSCP marked as EF, and steered to MPLS if it meets latency and jitter targets. A common misconception is that control and data policies do the same thing; they do not—control policies shape route advertisement, whereas data policies shape actual packet forwarding and real‑time steering. By the end you'll be able to design AAR sequences, set QoS marking, and define zone rules with an eye toward testing and safe rollout.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives orient your work with centralized data policies in SD‑WAN and show practical outcomes. First, you'll explain how centralized data policies differ from control policies and how they influence packet forwarding on vEdge and cEdge devices. Knowing this distinction helps you design correct match-action sequences. Second, you'll configure Application‑Aware Routing by defining application groups and SLA classes so traffic is steered dynamically to links that meet performance targets. Third, you'll implement QoS centrally—classifying flows, setting DSCP values, and applying policing or shaping—to protect latency-sensitive workloads. Fourth, you'll design zone-based firewall rules centrally to segment traffic and permit or deny flows between LAN, WAN, and DMZ. For each objective you'll practice a concise verification step, such as checking traffic classification in vManage or validating SLA failover in a lab. These skills are essential because they convert policy intent into edge behavior that preserves application experience and enforces security consistently across a distributed fabric.

screens.title: How you'll validate and test
screens.narratorSegment: Validation is as important as design. For centralized data policies, you will verify correct behavior in vManage and at the branch. When explaining policy roles, check that vSmart distributes the policy and that vEdge shows the active configuration. For AAR, build test cases that emulate degraded links and confirm voice or video sessions fail over to the preferred color according to SLA settings. For QoS, generate traffic to exceed a configured threshold and observe DSCP marking and queueing behavior. For security rules, use targeted flows such as HTTPS to internal servers to ensure accept rules work and unwanted applications are dropped. A frequent mistake is trusting policy syntax without observing traffic-level effects. Always run a simple traffic capture or use vManage monitoring to confirm DPI classification, SLA evaluation, and DSCP propagation. These verification steps give you confidence that the centrally defined intent becomes the network's live behavior.

screens.title: What is a Centralized Data Policy?
screens.narratorSegment: A Centralized Data Policy is a set of match and action rules authored in vManage, distributed by vSmart, and enforced by vEdge or cEdge devices to control real‑time packet forwarding. Unlike control policies that influence route advertisement and topology, data policies live on the data plane and make per‑flow decisions such as assigning an SLA class, setting DSCP, or applying a firewall rule. For example, you can match SIP and RTP packets, set them to an SLA that requires latency under 100 milliseconds, mark them EF for expedited forwarding, and instruct the edge to prefer MPLS when the SLA is met. Important misconceptions include thinking data policies only change routes: they also mark and queue packets and can drop or log flows. Another common error is assuming order doesn't matter; data policies are processed in sequence and the first match wins. Key takeaway: design explicit, ordered match statements, validate DPI classifications, and test fallback behavior before rolling out to production. What is a Centralized Data Policy? means a centrally authored rule set that enforces classification, sla assignment, dscp marking, steering, and security at the edge.. In practical terms, how data policies translate intent into per‑packet forwarding at the edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › What is a Centralized Data Policy?
Core definition
Centralized data policies are authored on vManage and enforce behavior on the data plane at the edge devices.
Primary actions
  • Assign SLA class to flows for AAR
  • Set DSCP values and forwarding classes for QoS
  • Apply zone-based firewall rules and logging
Sequence model
Policies are processed sequentially. The first matching sequence takes effect.
Common misconception
Data policies do more than route selection; they change per‑packet marks and can drop or log traffic.
Concrete example
Match SIP/RTP → Set SLA_Voice → Mark DSCP EF → Prefer MPLS if SLA met; fallback order defines alternate TLOCs.
Key Takeaway
Centralized policies convert intent into enforcement on every packet at the branch.

screens.title: How data policies are distributed and applied
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distribution path for centralized data policies prevents confusion during troubleshooting. The authoring begins in vManage where you create application groups, SLA classes, and the traffic data policy sequences. After you commit the policy, vManage pushes it to vSmart, which distributes the policy set to the relevant vEdge or cEdge devices. At the edge, the data policy is applied on the data plane to classify traffic, assign SLA classes, set DSCP, and apply security rules. A concrete example: you create an AAR policy in vManage to match Voice_Apps and set SLA_Voice. After pushing, vSmart sends the policy to all branch routers designated in the site list. Each vEdge then continually evaluates SLA probes on its TLOCs and makes per‑flow steering decisions. A common mistake is assuming distribution implies immediate global enforcement; propagation and local evaluation are two steps—if vSmart distribution fails or the edge lacks the SLA probes configured correctly, enforcement will not behave as expected. The practical takeaway is to monitor vManage, vSmart distribution status, and vEdge policy tables to confirm successful rollout. How data policies are distributed and applied means vmanage → vsmart → vedge/cedge. authoring, distribution, and local evaluation are distinct phases to verify.. In practical terms, from vmanage authoring to enforcement at vedge/cedge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Distribution & Enforcement
Process: Author → Distribute → Enforce
  1. Authoring: Create application groups, SLA classes, and sequences in vManage.
  2. Push: vManage sends the policy to vSmart for distribution.
  3. Distribution: vSmart distributes policies to targeted vEdge/cEdge devices.
  4. Local evaluation: Edges use SLA probes and DPI to make per‑flow decisions in real time.
Practical check: Confirm vSmart distribution status in vManage and then verify the active policy and SLA probe outcomes on an example vEdge.
Concrete scenario
You author an AAR policy that matches Voice_Apps and sets SLA_Voice. After deployment, the branch vEdge shows the sequence active and begins measuring latency and jitter for each TLOC. When MPLS meets SLA_Voice the edge steers active voice flows to MPLS; if MPLS degrades, the edge switches to the next preferred color in the fallback order.
Common mistake
Skipping SLA probe configuration or not scoping the site list; edges then lack the measurements to act.
Pro tip
Use a small test site for initial policy rollouts to observe real probe results before broad deployment.

screens.title: Application‑Aware Routing (AAR) defined
screens.narratorSegment: Application‑Aware Routing is a data policy function that steers application flows based on real‑time transport performance against predefined SLA thresholds. The AAR engine watches latency, jitter, and packet loss for each transport TLOC and matches flows to SLA classes you defined. For example, set SLA_Voice with latency less than 100 milliseconds and jitter less than 30 milliseconds. When a voice flow matches, the edge prefers the first transport in the policy's preferred path order that meets SLA_Voice. A concrete example: voice calls normally use MPLS; if MPLS fails the SLA, AAR directs voice to a business internet or LTE path that meets the SLA. Common misconceptions include thinking AAR is static—it's dynamic and continuous—and assuming it replaces QoS; AAR steers flows while QoS ensures packets are prioritized on the selected link. The practical takeaway: define realistic SLA thresholds, order fallback colors intentionally, and validate with synthetic traffic and monitoring so AAR can preserve application experience under real network conditions. Application‑Aware Routing (AAR) defined means continuously evaluate link metrics and choose the first transport that satisfies the sla for that application group.. In practical terms, steering application traffic using sla classes and live link metrics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AAR steers by SLA
keyIdea.text: Continuously evaluate link metrics and choose the first transport that satisfies the SLA for that application group.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Application-Aware Routing
What AAR does
AAR evaluates live transport metrics and assigns traffic to the first transport that meets a defined SLA class.
SLA example
SLA_Voice: Latency < 100ms, Jitter < 30ms, Packet loss < 1%
Fallback
Define preferred path order (e.g., mpls, biz-internet, lte) for deterministic fallback when a primary fails SLA.
Concrete walkthrough
You match Voice_Apps, set SLA_Voice, and configure the policy to prefer MPLS. The edge measures TLOCs and, for each active flow, chooses the first color meeting SLA_Voice. If none meet it, the policy can fall back to a best-effort class. Monitor call MOS or user reports while you tune thresholds.
Misconception
AAR isn't QoS—it chooses the path; QoS must still prioritize packets on that path.
Check
Use vManage monitoring to view SLA probe results and observe dynamic steering during link degradation tests.

screens.title: Creating an AAR policy: step by step
screens.narratorSegment: To implement AAR you'll follow a clear sequence: define application groups, create SLA classes, author the traffic data policy with sequences, and then apply the policy to the appropriate sites and VPNs. Start by grouping similar apps—Voice_Apps and Video_Apps—so one policy can target several protocols consistently. Next, create SLA classes with realistic thresholds: for voice, latency under 100 milliseconds, jitter under 30 milliseconds, and packet loss under 1 percent; for video, slightly looser thresholds. Then author sequences in the traffic data policy where each sequence matches an application list and sets the SLA class, including preferred path order for fallback. Finally, apply to All_WAN_Edges or to a site list and push the policy. A concrete example is an AAR policy that sets SLA_Voice for Voice_Apps and prefers MPLS, with LTE as a later fallback. A common pitfall is setting unrealistically tight SLAs that cause constant failover; tune thresholds from monitored performance and test using synthetic traffic before full deployment. Creating an AAR policy: step by step means app groups → sla classes → traffic policy sequences → apply to sites; tune slas and test before rollout.. In practical terms, define application groups, sla classes, and the policy sequences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › AAR Implementation Steps
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Define Application Groups (e.g., Voice_Apps, Video_Apps).
  2. Create SLA Classes with measurable thresholds.
  3. Author Traffic Data Policy sequences that match app lists and set SLA classes.
  4. Specify preferred path order and default action for unmatched traffic.
  5. Apply policy scope (site list, VPNs) and push configuration.
Pro tip: Start with a conservative SLA and test with simulated load to avoid unnecessary failovers.
Concrete example
Sequence 10: Match Voice_Apps → Set SLA_Voice → Preferred order: mpls, biz-internet, lte. Sequence 20: Match Video_Apps → Set SLA_Video → Preferred order: lte, biz-internet, mpls. Default: Best_Effort.
Validation
After deployment, monitor probe results and call quality metrics to refine thresholds and fallback ordering.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › AAR Policy Snippet
Conceptual AAR Policy (GUI equivalent)
# Example AAR Policy (Conceptual, configured in vManage GUI)

Policy Name: App_Aware_Routing_Policy

VPN List: All_VPNs
Site List: All_WAN_Edges

Traffic Data Policy:
  Sequence 10:
    Match:
      Application List: Voice_Apps
    Action:
      Set SLA Class: SLA_Voice
      # Preferred path order: mpls, biz-internet, lte

  Sequence 20:
    Match:
      Application List: Video_Apps
    Action:
      Set SLA Class: SLA_Video
      # Preferred path order: lte, biz-internet, mpls

  Default Action:
    Set SLA Class: Default_SLA (best-effort)
Walkthrough
Sequence 10 specifically matches voice flows and tags them for SLA evaluation. The edge will probe TLOCs and pick the first color meeting SLA_Voice. Sequence order ensures voice is evaluated before video.
Misconfiguration risk
If application lists are incomplete or DPI misidentifies apps, matches will not occur and traffic will fall to the default SLA.

screens.title: SLA classes and thresholds
screens.narratorSegment: SLA classes are the rules that define acceptable performance for groups of applications. Each class specifies thresholds for latency, jitter, and packet loss. For instance, SLA_Voice might require latency under 100 milliseconds, jitter under 30 milliseconds, and packet loss under 1 percent. SLA_Video can use looser values. The edge compares real‑time probe measurements to these thresholds to decide whether a path meets the SLA. When multiple TLOCs meet an SLA, the policy's preferred path order determines which one is chosen. If no TLOC meets the SLA, the edge can fall back to a lower‑priority SLA or default best‑effort behavior. A common misconception is treating SLA thresholds as absolute guarantees; they are engineering targets used to guide steering and must be tuned per site. A practical strategy is to baseline real link performance, set SLAs slightly above observed good performance, and then monitor failover frequency. The takeaway is to design SLAs pragmatically so AAR makes useful, not disruptive, steering decisions. SLA classes and thresholds means sla classes set measurable thresholds; realistic tuning avoids excessive failover and preserves user experience.. In practical terms, designing sla thresholds and fallback behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: SLA classes are the rules that define acceptable performance for groups of applications. Each class specifies thresholds for latency, jitter, and packet loss. For instance, SLA_Voice might require latency under 100 milliseconds, jitter under 30 milliseconds, and packet loss under 1 percent. SLA_Video can use looser values. The edge compares real‑time probe measurements to these thresholds to decide whether a path meets the SLA. When multiple TLOCs meet an SLA, the policy's preferred path order determines which one is chosen. If no TLOC meets the SLA, the edge can fall back to a lower‑priority SLA or default best‑effort behavior. A common misconception is treating SLA thresholds as absolute guarantees; they are engineering targets used to guide steering and must be tuned per site. A practical strategy is to baseline real link performance, set SLAs slightly above observed good performance, and then monitor failover frequency. The takeaway is to design SLAs pragmatically so AAR makes useful, not disruptive, steering decisions. SLA classes and thresholds means sla classes set measurable thresholds; realistic tuning avoids excessive failover and preserves user experience.. In practical terms, designing sla thresholds and fallback behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › SLA Classes
Designing SLA classes
Set latency, jitter, and packet loss thresholds that match application needs and observed link behavior.
SLA_Voice: Latency < 100ms; Jitter < 30ms; Loss < 1%
SLA_Video: Latency < 200ms; Jitter < 50ms; Loss < 2%
Fallback behavior
If primary TLOC fails SLA, try next color in the preferred list or fall back to a lower SLA.
Concrete tuning approach
Measure baseline latency and jitter for each transport. Set SLA slightly above baseline good performance to avoid unnecessary failovers. Monitor and adjust based on real user experience.
Misconception
Don't set SLAs so tight that normal variance triggers constant switching; this degrades experience rather than improving it.

screens.title: QoS mechanisms in SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: Quality of Service in SD‑WAN uses classification, marking, and egress controls to protect application performance across transports. First, classify traffic by application, IP, port, or DSCP. The SD‑WAN DPI engine enables accurate classification beyond simple port numbers. Next, mark packets with a DSCP value; for voice, EF (46) is commonly used to signal expedited forwarding through downstream devices. Then assign forwarding classes or queuing behavior so marked packets get prioritized on congested links. Finally, use policing or shaping at the egress to enforce bandwidth limits: policing drops traffic exceeding a configured rate, while shaping buffers and smooths bursts to reduce drops. A concrete example is classifying Voice_Apps, marking DSCP EF, assigning the Voice forwarding class, and reserving a percentage of TLOC bandwidth for that class. Misconceptions include thinking DSCP alone guarantees end‑to‑end behavior; downstream devices must honor DSCP and queues must be configured. The practical takeaway is to combine accurate classification with consistent marking and queue configuration across the fabric and to validate with traffic tests. QoS mechanisms in SD‑WAN means classification + dscp + forwarding class + policing/shaping ensure critical flows are prioritized consistently.. In practical terms, classification, dscp marking, policing, and shaping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › QoS Mechanisms
QoS building blocks
  • Classification: Identify traffic by DPI, ports, or IPs.
  • Marking (DSCP): Set DSCP values like EF (46) for voice.
  • Forwarding class/Queuing: Map marks to priority queues and reserved bandwidth.
  • Policing/Shaping: Enforce or smooth traffic at egress to control bursts.
Example policy behavior
Match Voice_Apps → Set DSCP EF (46) → Assign Forwarding Class: Voice → Reserve bandwidth or shaping at egress. Under congestion, voice receives prioritized processing and lower classes are delayed or dropped first.
Misconception
DSCP marking alone does not enforce scheduling—intermediate devices must honor DSCP and queues must be configured end-to-end.

screens.title: Conceptual QoS policy snippet
screens.narratorSegment: This is a conceptual QoS data policy you might create in vManage to protect voice and video. Sequences match application groups and set DSCP and forwarding class attributes accordingly. For voice, set DSCP to EF (46) and earmark bandwidth; for video, use AF41. The policy shown is a logical representation—actual configuration in vManage will use GUI fields—but it communicates the order of operations: classify, mark, and map to forwarding behavior. A common pitfall is applying restrictive policing without reserving enough bandwidth, which can lead to voice drops under load. Another oversight is forgetting to set local TLOC bandwidth or shaping on the egress, reducing the effectiveness of queueing. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › QoS Policy Snippet
Conceptual QoS Policy
# Example QoS Policy (Conceptual, configured in vManage GUI)

Policy Name: Branch_QoS

VPN List: All_VPNs
Site List: Branch_Sites

Traffic Data Policy:
  Sequence 10:
    Match:
      Application List: Voice_Apps
    Action:
      Set DSCP: EF (46)
      # Set Forwarding Class: Voice
      # Set Local TLOC Bandwidth: 1000kbps (for this class)

  Sequence 20:
    Match:
      Application List: Video_Apps
    Action:
      Set DSCP: AF41 (34)
      # Set Forwarding Class: Video

  Default Action:
    Set DSCP: BE (0)
    # Set Forwarding Class: Best_Effort
Walkthrough
Sequence 10 ensures voice is marked and mapped to the voice queue. Reserve bandwidth so policing doesn't starve voice. Sequence order ensures voice classification is evaluated before general video or best-effort matches.
Common mistake
Applying strict policing without shaping or bandwidth reservations can cause higher drop rates for sensitive traffic during bursts.

screens.title: Zone‑based firewall as a centralized data policy
screens.narratorSegment: Zone‑based firewall policies can be authored centrally and distributed as data policies to provide consistent, edge‑enforced segmentation. You define zone lists—such as LAN_Zone, WAN_Zone, and DMZ—and then create zone pairs with ordered sequences of match and action statements. For example, a rule from LAN_Zone to WAN_Zone can accept HTTPS to internal servers while another sequence drops unwanted P2P applications. Rule order matters: place specific deny sequences before general accept rules. A useful concrete example is permitting internal clients to reach an internal HTTPS server while dropping P2P traffic and logging those events. Misconfigurations often arise from overly broad allow rules placed earlier in the sequence, which can inadvertently permit traffic that later rules are intended to block. The practical takeaway is to design narrowly scoped rules, test them in a lab, and use logging to confirm the DPI matches and sequence evaluation behave as intended before broad deployment. Zone‑based firewall as a centralized data policy means define zones and ordered rules centrally; specific denies must come before broad permits to avoid unintended access.. In practical terms, defining zones, zone pairs, and ordered rules to segment and protect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Zone-Based Firewall
Zone-based firewall basics
Define logical zones and control traffic between them with ordered rules applied at the edge.
Zone List examples: LAN_Zone (VPN0, VPN10), WAN_Zone (TLOCs), DMZ_Zone.
Rule order
Place specific deny rules before general accept rules to avoid accidental allowances.
Concrete policy example
# Example Zone-Based Firewall Policy (Conceptual)

Policy Name: Branch_Firewall

VPN List: All_VPNs
Site List: Branch_Sites

Zone List: LAN_Zone (VPN 0, VPN 10), WAN_Zone (TLOCs)

Security Policy:
  Zone Pair: LAN_Zone to WAN_Zone
    Sequence 10:
      Match:
        Source Data Prefix List: Internal_Servers (10.0.0.0/24)
        Destination Port: 443
      Action:
        Accept
        Log: True
    Sequence 20:
      Match:
        Application List: P2P_Apps
      Action:
        Drop
        Log: True
    Default Action:
      Drop
Validate with test flows and logging. A broad default-drop protects the zone pair but ensure required accepts are configured first.

screens.title: How data policies interact with transport links
screens.narratorSegment: The interaction between data policies and transport links is where centralized policies deliver value. Edges run SLA probes that measure latency, jitter, and packet loss for each TLOC. The AAR engine compares these measurements to SLA classes and chooses the first transport color in the preferred order that meets the thresholds. For example, a voice flow will use MPLS while it meets SLA_Voice; if MPLS degrades, the edge checks the next color such as biz-internet or LTE. Early warning signs include frequent flapping between transports or many flows being steered to best-effort because SLAs are too strict. These are indications to revisit thresholds, probe intervals, or link configurations. A concrete troubleshooting approach is: confirm SLA probe configuration, inspect per-TLOC probe stats, check DPI classification for the affected flows, and validate that the preferred path order is what you intended. The practical takeaway is that robust monitoring and realistic SLA tuning are essential to let AAR enhance resilience rather than cause instability. How data policies interact with transport links means sla probes and preferred path order govern steering; tune thresholds and monitor to avoid oscillation.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Edges send probes to measure latency, jitter, and loss per TLOC.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on centralized data policies and why they are the heart of SD‑WAN forwarding decisions. Centralized data policies are configured in vManage, distributed by vSmart, and enforced at the edge by vEdge or cEdge devices. These policies act on the data plane: they classify traffic, assign SLA expectations, mark packets for QoS, and implement security rules like zone‑based firewalls. You will learn how Application‑Aware Routing uses SLA classes to pick the best transport, how QoS uses classification and DSCP marking to prioritize flows, and how firewall zone pairs protect branches. A concrete example you'll see repeatedly is prioritizing Voice traffic: voice is identified, set to an SLA class, DSCP marked as EF, and steered to MPLS if it meets latency and jitter targets. A common misconception is that control and data policies do the same thing; they do not—control policies shape route advertisement, whereas data policies shape actual packet forwarding and real‑time steering. By the end you'll be able to design AAR sequences, set QoS marking, and define zone rules with an eye toward testing and safe rollout.

These objectives orient your work with centralized data policies in SD‑WAN and show practical outcomes. First, you'll explain how centralized data policies differ from control policies and how they influence packet forwarding on vEdge and cEdge devices. Knowing this distinction helps you design correct match-action sequences. Second, you'll configure Application‑Aware Routing by defining application groups and SLA classes so traffic is steered dynamically to links that meet performance targets. Third, you'll implement QoS centrally—classifying flows, setting DSCP values, and applying policing or shaping—to protect latency-sensitive workloads. Fourth, you'll design zone-based firewall rules centrally to segment traffic and permit or deny flows between LAN, WAN, and DMZ. For each objective you'll practice a concise verification step, such as checking traffic classification in vManage or validating SLA failover in a lab. These skills are essential because they convert policy intent into edge behavior that preserves application experience and enforces security consistently across a distributed fabric.

Validation is as important as design. For centralized data policies, you will verify correct behavior in vManage and at the branch. When explaining policy roles, check that vSmart distributes the policy and that vEdge shows the active configuration. For AAR, build test cases that emulate degraded links and confirm voice or video sessions fail over to the preferred color according to SLA settings. For QoS, generate traffic to exceed a configured threshold and observe DSCP marking and queueing behavior. For security rules, use targeted flows such as HTTPS to internal servers to ensure accept rules work and unwanted applications are dropped. A frequent mistake is trusting policy syntax without observing traffic-level effects. Always run a simple traffic capture or use vManage monitoring to confirm DPI classification, SLA evaluation, and DSCP propagation. These verification steps give you confidence that the centrally defined intent becomes the network's live behavior.

A Centralized Data Policy is a set of match and action rules authored in vManage, distributed by vSmart, and enforced by vEdge or cEdge devices to control real‑time packet forwarding. Unlike control policies that influence route advertisement and topology, data policies live on the data plane and make per‑flow decisions such as assigning an SLA class, setting DSCP, or applying a firewall rule. For example, you can match SIP and RTP packets, set them to an SLA that requires latency under 100 milliseconds, mark them EF for expedited forwarding, and instruct the edge to prefer MPLS when the SLA is met. Important misconceptions include thinking data policies only change routes: they also mark and queue packets and can drop or log flows. Another common error is assuming order doesn't matter; data policies are processed in sequence and the first match wins. Key takeaway: design explicit, ordered match statements, validate DPI classifications, and test fallback behavior before rolling out to production. What is a Centralized Data Policy? means a centrally authored rule set that enforces classification, sla assignment, dscp marking, steering, and security at the edge.. In practical terms, how data policies translate intent into per‑packet forwarding at the edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the distribution path for centralized data policies prevents confusion during troubleshooting. The authoring begins in vManage where you create application groups, SLA classes, and the traffic data policy sequences. After you commit the policy, vManage pushes it to vSmart, which distributes the policy set to the relevant vEdge or cEdge devices. At the edge, the data policy is applied on the data plane to classify traffic, assign SLA classes, set DSCP, and apply security rules. A concrete example: you create an AAR policy in vManage to match Voice_Apps and set SLA_Voice. After pushing, vSmart sends the policy to all branch routers designated in the site list. Each vEdge then continually evaluates SLA probes on its TLOCs and makes per‑flow steering decisions. A common mistake is assuming distribution implies immediate global enforcement; propagation and local evaluation are two steps—if vSmart distribution fails or the edge lacks the SLA probes configured correctly, enforcement will not behave as expected. The practical takeaway is to monitor vManage, vSmart distribution status, and vEdge policy tables to confirm successful rollout. How data policies are distributed and applied means vmanage → vsmart → vedge/cedge. authoring, distribution, and local evaluation are distinct phases to verify.. In practical terms, from vmanage authoring to enforcement at vedge/cedge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Application‑Aware Routing is a data policy function that steers application flows based on real‑time transport performance against predefined SLA thresholds. The AAR engine watches latency, jitter, and packet loss for each transport TLOC and matches flows to SLA classes you defined. For example, set SLA_Voice with latency less than 100 milliseconds and jitter less than 30 milliseconds. When a voice flow matches, the edge prefers the first transport in the policy's preferred path order that meets SLA_Voice. A concrete example: voice calls normally use MPLS; if MPLS fails the SLA, AAR directs voice to a business internet or LTE path that meets the SLA. Common misconceptions include thinking AAR is static—it's dynamic and continuous—and assuming it replaces QoS; AAR steers flows while QoS ensures packets are prioritized on the selected link. The practical takeaway: define realistic SLA thresholds, order fallback colors intentionally, and validate with synthetic traffic and monitoring so AAR can preserve application experience under real network conditions. Application‑Aware Routing (AAR) defined means continuously evaluate link metrics and choose the first transport that satisfies the sla for that application group.. In practical terms, steering application traffic using sla classes and live link metrics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To implement AAR you'll follow a clear sequence: define application groups, create SLA classes, author the traffic data policy with sequences, and then apply the policy to the appropriate sites and VPNs. Start by grouping similar apps—Voice_Apps and Video_Apps—so one policy can target several protocols consistently. Next, create SLA classes with realistic thresholds: for voice, latency under 100 milliseconds, jitter under 30 milliseconds, and packet loss under 1 percent; for video, slightly looser thresholds. SLA classes are the rules that define acceptable performance for groups of applications. Each class specifies thresholds for latency, jitter, and packet loss. For instance, SLA_Voice might require latency under 100 milliseconds, jitter under 30 milliseconds, and packet loss under 1 percent. SLA_Video can use looser values. The edge compares real‑time probe measurements to these thresholds to decide whether a path meets the SLA. When multiple TLOCs meet an SLA, the policy's preferred path order determines which one is chosen. If no TLOC meets the SLA, the edge can fall back to a lower‑priority SLA or default best‑effort behavior. A common misconception is treating SLA thresholds as absolute guarantees; they are engineering targets used to guide steering and must be tuned per site. A practical strategy is to baseline real link performance, set SLAs slightly above observed good performance, and then monitor failover frequency. The takeaway is to design SLAs pragmatically so AAR makes useful, not disruptive, steering decisions. The interaction between data policies and transport links is where centralized policies deliver value. Edges run SLA probes that measure latency, jitter, and packet loss for each TLOC. The AAR engine compares these measurements to SLA classes and chooses the first transport color in the preferred order that meets the thresholds. For example, a voice flow will use MPLS while it meets SLA_Voice; if MPLS degrades, the edge checks the next color such as biz-internet or LTE.
